lessons.title: Enterprise, Entrepreneurs & Risk and Reward
lessons.description: What enterprise is, what makes an entrepreneur, and the risk-reward trade-off at the heart of starting up.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do People Start Businesses?

Every business on your high street — the coffee shop, the barber, the phone repair kiosk — began when one person looked at the world and said ‘I could do that better.’ The specification frames this through enterprise: the act of spotting a gap, developing an idea and turning it into a business that customers will actually pay for. Enterprise is built on three linked steps — spotting an opportunity, developing an idea, and satisfying the needs of customers.

An opportunity is a gap in the market — a problem customers want solved, or a product they wish existed. James Watt noticed in 2007 that UK pubs sold bland mass-market lagers while US drinkers were enjoying flavourful craft beers, so he co-founded BrewDog in Aberdeen. Ben Francis noticed in 2012 that gym-goers wanted fitted sportswear, not baggy football shirts, so he sewed the first Gymshark tops in his parents’ Solihull garage.

Once the opportunity is spotted, the entrepreneur has to develop an idea that actually works — a product people want, at a price that covers costs. Finally, the business must satisfy customer needs: the product has to deliver, the service has to be reliable, and the customer has to come back. Enterprise is not just the idea; it is the delivery.

Key Fact

Enterprise has three steps: spotting an opportunity, developing an idea, and satisfying customer needs. Without all three, a business idea stays a daydream — delivery is what turns it into a business.

What Makes an Entrepreneur?

An entrepreneur is the person who carries the idea through. The specification names four characteristics: creativity, risk taking, determination and confidence. Creativity is the ability to see what others miss — Sir James Dyson noticed his vacuum losing suction, so he designed the bagless cyclone. Risk taking is the willingness to put your own money, time and reputation on the line when success is not guaranteed. Determination is the grit to keep going through setbacks — Dyson built 5,127 failed prototypes before the DC01 went on sale. Confidence is the self-belief to pitch the idea to banks, investors and customers even when no one has heard of you yet.

Sara Davies founded Crafter’s Companion at 21 while still a student, pitched her own invention — an envelope-making tool — on QVC, and built a multi-million-pound business before joining the Dragons’ Den. She needed every one of the four traits: creativity to design the product, risk to borrow against it, determination to keep going when retailers said no, and confidence to go on live TV to sell it.

Research suggests most entrepreneurial traits can be learned. Young Enterprise programmes, the National Enterprise Network, and university start-up schemes all train the four characteristics in teenagers who would not have called themselves entrepreneurial at 14. Watching Dragons’ Den is not a substitute for actually building something, but it models the behaviours — rehearsing a pitch, thinking about numbers, handling rejection — that every founder eventually needs.

The Concept of Risk and Reward

Every business decision is a trade between risk and reward. Starting a business is the clearest example. The risks are real and personal: savings invested may be lost, a guaranteed salary is given up, a home may be mortgaged to raise finance, and long hours replace evenings and weekends. If the idea fails, sole traders and partners face unlimited liability — creditors can pursue personal assets. The rewards run wider than profit: independence (being your own boss), satisfaction (solving a problem you care about), the chance to build something lasting, and the potential upside if the business grows.

Sir James Dyson’s story shows both halves. In the 1980s he remortgaged his house and spent more than a decade refining his bagless vacuum idea. Five retailers turned him down before Japan stocked the prototype — without that sale, he would have lost everything. The reward was a company now valued in the billions, but the risk almost broke him first.

Key Fact

Risk and reward run through every business decision. Risks include losing savings, giving up a secure salary and unlimited liability. Rewards include profit, independence, personal satisfaction and the chance to build something that lasts.

Balancing Risk and Reward

Entrepreneurs do not avoid risk — they manage it. A good business plan, market research before launch, starting small before scaling, and keeping a cash reserve all reduce risk without killing ambition. Ben Francis kept working part-time in a pizza delivery job in Gymshark’s early years so the start-up did not need to cover his wages. Pasta Evangelists trialled its fresh-pasta subscription in London before shipping nationwide. Each of these choices keeps the potential reward intact while cutting the downside if the idea stalls.

Risk and reward return in section 7 of the course — the interdependent nature of business. Every decision in marketing, operations, finance and people is a version of the same trade: what could go wrong, what could go right, and is the upside worth the exposure? Keep that lens sharp; you will reuse it.

UK government data shows around 40% of new businesses close within three years, usually because cash runs out before sales grow big enough to cover costs. The common causes are under-estimating how long it takes to win customers, over-estimating how much profit margins will be, and taking on personal debt the founder cannot service if sales slip. An entrepreneur who understands these risks builds a cushion — keeps a part-time job, delays big hires, and launches with a minimum viable product rather than a full range.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For OCR questions on risk and reward, avoid listing rewards only as ‘profit’. Mark schemes reward candidates who identify non-financial rewards too — independence, satisfaction, flexibility, building something lasting. On 6-mark Analyse questions about entrepreneurs, tie each characteristic (creativity, risk taking, determination, confidence) to a specific feature of the named business in the case study, then develop one consequence per trait. Remember Section A gives you 15 guaranteed marks — attempt every multiple choice even when unsure.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Enterprise means spotting an opportunity, developing an idea and satisfying customer needs — all three steps have to work for a business to succeed.
  • Entrepreneurs share four characteristics: creativity, risk taking, determination and confidence — most can be learned with practice, not just inherited.
  • Risk and reward underpin every business decision — rewards include profit, independence and satisfaction; risks include lost savings, unlimited liability and long hours.

practice_questions.text: Outline one risk an entrepreneur takes when starting a new business. (Context: Aisha is leaving her job as a salaried graphic designer to set up her own freelance branding studio in Manchester, using £12,000 of personal savings as start-up capital.)

2 marks: adds development with application to Aisha — e.g. ‘Aisha is giving up her guaranteed designer salary (1), so if client work is slow in the first few months she will have no regular income and may need to use the £12,000 savings to cover her rent (1).’

practice_questions.text: Explain one way creativity helps an entrepreneur to develop a successful business idea. (Context: Sir James Dyson designed the world’s first bagless vacuum cleaner after noticing his own vacuum losing suction.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies creativity as seeing a problem others miss (AO1).
2 marks: applies creativity to the Dyson example (AO2) — e.g. noticing the suction issue in his own home.
3 marks: develops the consequence for the business — the cyclone solved a widespread customer problem, giving Dyson a genuinely new product with no direct rival.
Indicative answer: ‘Creativity allows an entrepreneur to spot a problem that rivals have ignored (1). Sir James Dyson noticed his own vacuum losing suction and invented the bagless cyclone as a solution (2), which gave him a genuinely different product and a gap in the market with no direct rival (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how risk and reward might influence the decision of an entrepreneur to leave their job and start their own business. (Context: Dan, 28, earns £32,000 as a head chef. He is considering leaving to open his own street-food burger van using £18,000 of personal savings.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning anchored to Dan’s case. Chain 1 (risk): giving up £32,000 salary + using £18,000 savings → unlimited liability as a sole trader → personal assets exposed if the van fails → specific consequence (e.g. Dan could lose his whole savings cushion and struggle to pay rent). Chain 2 (reward): independence / full profits / doing work he loves → potential for higher earnings than salary if the van succeeds → ability to grow the idea into a second van. Sustained application to Dan.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear application to Dan at key steps, reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but not fully linked to Dan; some context used but generic in places.
Emerging: Lists risks and rewards abstractly without applying them to the case study. A generic answer with no application to Dan cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether the rewards of starting a new business always outweigh the risks for a first-time entrepreneur. (Context: two recent university graduates in Leeds are choosing between (A) accepting graduate jobs paying £28,000 each or (B) pooling their £10,000 combined savings to launch a subscription fresh-juice delivery service.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument developing both sides with reference to the graduates’ specific circumstances (small savings, no business track record, two graduate jobs foregone). Reaches a supported judgement that weighs one side more heavily, or says ‘it depends on X’ with X justified (e.g. depends on whether they can keep one graduate salary as a safety net).
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear judgement, some application to the graduates.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, judgement restates earlier points without weighting.
Emerging: One-sided argument, no judgement, or no application to the case.

Arguments that rewards outweigh risks: independence, potential upside of a successful start-up (Gymshark valuation), early-career years are the easiest time to take risk (no mortgage, no children).
Arguments that risks outweigh rewards: giving up £56,000 combined graduate salary, only £10,000 capital is thin, unlimited liability as sole traders / partners, high early-stage failure rate, no business experience.
Strong judgements note that launching while one graduate keeps a salary, or trialling the subscription part-time before quitting, would cut the risk without killing the reward. [9 marks]

lessons.title: Business Planning
lessons.description: What a business plan does, what goes in it, and how it reduces risk and helps secure finance.
lessons.content_html:
The Purpose of Planning

A good idea by itself is not a business — it is a hope. The step that turns the idea into a venture someone will lend money to, and that rivals will have to take seriously, is a written plan. A business plan forces the entrepreneur to answer the awkward questions early: who will buy this, for how much, against whom, and with what money? The specification says the purpose of planning business activity is to reduce risk and help the business succeed. Both matter, and both flow from the same document.

Planning reduces risk because the process itself flushes out hidden problems. Writing down your expected sales forces you to check your market research. Drafting your forecast costs makes you ring suppliers for real prices. Adding a cash flow forecast reveals the month when money will be tightest. None of these problems go away because they are ignored — but they are cheaper to fix on paper than after launch.

Key Fact

The two purposes of planning business activity are to reduce risk and to help the business succeed. Writing the plan forces entrepreneurs to answer awkward questions early — before the money is at stake.

What Goes Inside a Business Plan

A typical business plan runs to 15–30 pages and contains a standard set of sections. The executive summary opens with the one-paragraph pitch — what the business is, who it serves, and why it will work. The market section lays out target customers, market size and main competitors, with evidence drawn from market research. The operations section explains how the product will actually be made or delivered — premises, suppliers, staff. The finance section contains the numbers: start-up costs, forecast sales, forecast profit and loss, and a cash flow forecast for the first year or two. The people section names the founders and any key hires and explains why this team can deliver. A short appendix holds CVs, research data and quotations from suppliers.

Each section has a job. The market section proves customers exist. The operations section proves the founders know how the product reaches them. The finance section proves the maths works. Skipping one leaves a question a lender or investor will immediately ask at interview.

A high-street business banker, or an angel investor like those on Dragons’ Den, rarely reads a plan cover to cover. They flick to the executive summary to decide whether the idea is worth further attention, then turn to the cash flow forecast to see when repayment is realistic and whether the headroom is enough if sales come in slow. Their third stop is the market evidence — does the demand actually exist? A plan that wins funding is one where those three answers are credible, specific and honest. Inflated sales forecasts are the fastest way to lose credibility.

The Role of the Plan — Identifying Markets and Resources

The specification lists four roles for a business plan once it has been written. It identifies markets — who the customers are, where they are and how many there might be. A cafe owner in Leeds who writes ‘everyone’ as her target customer has not identified a market; writing ‘office workers on Greek Street lunching between 12 and 2’ has.

The plan also identifies the resources the business needs to operate. Resources here means premises, equipment, stock, staff and start-up cash. A bakery needs ovens, a van, a shop lease, ingredients, two part-time counter staff and insurance — all of which cost real money, and all of which have to be found before the doors open. A plan that lists resources makes it obvious when the founder’s savings will not stretch and finance will be needed.

The Role of the Plan — Obtaining Finance and Achieving Objectives

A written plan helps finance in two ways. First, lenders almost always require one. No high-street bank will lend to a start-up without seeing a business plan with a realistic cash flow forecast. Second, a plan presents the idea credibly — an investor reading a plan with clear numbers, market evidence and supplier quotations is more willing to back the founder than one listening to an excited pitch across a kitchen table.

Finally, a plan helps the business achieve its aims and objectives — the SMART targets covered later in this unit. By writing objectives down and sequencing them against a timeline, the founder has a map: month three, break even on weekly sales; month six, hire a second baker; year two, open a second shop. Running without a plan is running without a compass: you may keep moving, but you will not know if you are getting closer to your destination.

Key Fact

A business plan has four roles: identifying markets, helping to obtain finance, identifying resources the business needs, and achieving aims and objectives. Skipping any one of them leaves a gap a lender or investor will notice.

Limitations of a Business Plan

A plan is useful, but it is not the business. Plans are written with forecasts — and forecasts are not facts. If the economy slows, if a rival opens nearby, or if a pandemic closes the high street, the numbers will be wrong. Plans can quickly go out of date: a plan written in January 2020 that assumed busy central London footfall was useless by April. Over-optimistic founders sometimes stretch the forecasts to win the loan, then struggle to hit numbers that were never realistic. A good plan is therefore a living document — reviewed every few months, adjusted when reality diverges, and not used as a straitjacket that forces the business down a road conditions no longer support.

Pasta Evangelists launched in 2016 with a plan to sell fresh pasta through a London subscription box. When the pandemic hit, the original plan — restaurant partnerships, office deliveries — fell apart. The founders rewrote the plan around home delivery nationwide and tripled in size during lockdown. The plan did its job not by being right, but by giving the business a clear baseline it could revise when the world shifted.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Explain questions on the role of a business plan, avoid the generic ‘it helps the business’. Name the specific role (identifying markets, obtaining finance, identifying resources, achieving objectives) and apply it to the named business in the stem. On 12-mark Evaluate questions asking whether a business plan is worth the effort, balance reduced risk and access to finance against the cost of the founder’s time and the certainty that forecasts will be wrong. A good judgement weighs one side rather than restating both.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Planning reduces risk and helps a business succeed by forcing founders to answer the awkward questions — customers, costs, competition — before launch.
  • A business plan has four roles: identifying markets, obtaining finance, identifying resources and achieving aims and objectives.
  • Plans have limitations — forecasts are uncertain and documents go out of date — so a good plan is reviewed regularly rather than filed away.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how writing a business plan can help a new entrepreneur to reduce the risk of failure. (Context: Leah is preparing to leave her office job to open an independent bookshop in Bristol. She has £22,000 in savings and is writing her first business plan.)

Chain 1: the plan forces market research → Leah confirms the catchment around her chosen Bristol street contains enough readers → reduces the risk of opening in the wrong location → named consequence (e.g. avoids signing a lease that sales cannot support). Chain 2: the plan forces a cash flow forecast → Leah sees that month 2 is her tightest month → arranges an overdraft in advance → protects her £22,000 savings from being wiped out by one bad month.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear application to Leah at key steps, at least one reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but loose application to Leah.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether writing a detailed business plan is always worth the effort for a first-time entrepreneur. (Context: Ade is planning to launch an online tutoring service from his bedroom. He has two weeks before term starts and is choosing between spending that time writing a 25-page plan or spending it on building the website and finding his first five clients.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument developing both sides, applied to Ade’s decision, with a supported judgement that either weights one side (e.g. ‘a lighter plan is enough when start-up capital is small’) or makes an explicit recommendation with evaluative comment.
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear judgement, some application to Ade.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, judgement restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported argument.

Arguments that a detailed plan IS worth it: forces market research, identifies resources, is required if Ade later needs finance, flushes out hidden costs (website hosting, DBS check, marketing), provides a yardstick for measuring his own progress.
Arguments against a detailed 25-page plan for Ade: his start-up cost is tiny so he does not need a bank loan, the market changes weekly during exam season, time spent writing is time not spent winning clients, forecasts for online tutoring are unreliable with no past sales data, a one-page plan may be enough.
Supported judgement: for Ade, a short written plan is valuable; a full 25-page document is not, because the risk reduction does not outweigh the opportunity cost of losing two weeks of client acquisition. [12 marks]

lessons.title: Business Ownership & Limited Liability
lessons.description: Sole traders, partnerships, Ltds and Plcs — features, suitability and what limited liability really means.
lessons.content_html:
Why Legal Structure Matters

Before a business trades, its owners have to decide what kind of organisation it will be. The legal structure chosen affects how much control the owners keep, how profits are shared, where the business can raise money, and crucially, what happens if things go wrong. A self-employed dog walker and Tesco PLC are both businesses, but they operate under very different rules. Choosing the wrong structure can cripple a good idea — so this decision is one of the first serious tests for any entrepreneur.

Sole Traders

A sole trader is a business with one owner. Think of a local plumber, a market-stall holder or a personal trainer. Setting up is simple: register with HMRC and start trading. The owner keeps all the profit and makes every decision. The downside is the same detail that makes it attractive — the owner is the business in the eyes of the law. They face unlimited liability, meaning if the business owes money it cannot repay, creditors can come after the owner’s house, car and savings.

Key Fact

Sole traders keep all the profit and have full control, but they have unlimited liability and limited ways to raise finance. Most UK businesses are sole traders — simple to set up, but risky if the business fails.

Partnerships

A partnership has between 2 and 20 owners who share the workload, combine their skills and pool capital. A high-street solicitor, a local accountancy firm and most GP surgeries run as partnerships. Decisions are shared, profits are split according to a partnership agreement, and more finance can be raised than by one individual. The drawback is that partners still have unlimited liability — and one partner’s mistake can land the others with the bill. Disagreements between partners also slow decisions.

Private Limited Companies (Ltd)

A private limited company (Ltd) is a separate legal entity owned by shareholders. Shares can be sold to family, friends or invited investors but not to the general public. Most UK companies with ‘Ltd’ at the end — Greggs was one before it floated, Dyson still is — fall into this category. The crucial advantage is limited liability. If the company goes bust, shareholders can only lose the money they put in; their personal assets are safe. In return, Ltds must register at Companies House and publish annual accounts.

Public Limited Companies (Plc)

A public limited company (Plc) can sell shares to the general public through the stock exchange. Tesco PLC, BT Group PLC and JD Sports Fashion PLC are household examples. Going public opens up huge sources of finance — millions of pounds can be raised in a single share issue — and raises brand profile. The catch: ownership is diluted, takeovers become possible, and every result is scrutinised by shareholders and the press. Plcs also face strict reporting and must publish detailed annual reports.

Both Ltds and Plcs have limited liability and are separate legal entities. The key difference is how they raise money. An Ltd can only sell shares to people it invites; a Plc can sell to anyone through the London Stock Exchange. That changes the scale of finance available — and the amount of outside control the owners must accept. When Aston Martin floated as a Plc in 2018, the founders accepted public scrutiny of every quarterly result in return for the cash to expand globally.

The decision to move from Ltd to Plc is called a flotation or Initial Public Offering (IPO). Many UK family businesses stay as Ltds precisely because they want to keep control inside the family. Going public is almost impossible to undo cheaply.

What Limited Liability Actually Means

Students regularly get this wrong in exams. Limited liability does NOT protect the business — the business can still go bust. What it protects is the owners. A shareholder who invested £5,000 can lose that £5,000 if the company collapses, but cannot be forced to sell their home to pay the company’s supplier invoices. With unlimited liability (sole traders and partnerships), creditors can. The mental image to hold is a wall between the shareholders’ personal money and the company’s debts. With Ltds and Plcs, that wall exists. With sole traders and partnerships, there is no wall.

Key Fact

Limited liability protects the owners’ personal assets — it does not protect the business itself. A company can still go bust; limited liability simply caps how much each shareholder can personally lose at the amount they invested.

Suitability in Different Business Contexts

Different stages and different contexts suit different structures. A lone builder just starting out will usually begin as a sole trader — cheap, simple, no reporting, and the work is low-risk enough to accept unlimited liability. Two dental graduates opening a practice together are suited to a partnership — they can share skills, pool savings and split the workload, and the patient risk is covered by professional indemnity insurance. A growing family catering business taking on larger corporate contracts will often become a private limited company to protect the owners’ homes from supplier claims if a major event goes wrong. A national retailer needing hundreds of millions of pounds to open stores will eventually list as a Plc.

Start-ups therefore tend to begin as sole traders or partnerships (low set-up cost, flexibility) and migrate to Ltd status as the business grows, the contracts get bigger and the need to protect personal assets rises. Established businesses with strong cash flow may stay private if keeping family control matters, or go public if they need growth capital that only the stock market can supply. There is no single ‘best’ structure — only the one that fits the size, risk level and finance needs of the business at this point in its life.

A typical UK journey: year one, market-stall baker operates as a sole trader; year three, she takes on a business partner and runs as a partnership; year five, they incorporate as an Ltd when they win their first supermarket contract and the supplier paperwork demands limited liability; year fifteen, if they want to open a chain of shops, they may raise expansion capital via a Plc flotation. Same founder, same product — but the right legal structure changes as the business scales and the risks change with it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Students lose marks on this topic by saying ‘the business has limited liability’. It doesn’t — the shareholders do. Write ‘the owners are only liable for what they invested’ instead. For Recommend questions asking you to choose a structure, always tie your choice to the specific business: a street-food van does not need Plc-level finance, and a multinational cannot run as a sole trader. Name the feature of the business (size, finance need, risk) that drives your choice.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sole traders and partnerships are simple to set up but carry unlimited liability — owners’ personal assets are at risk if the business fails.
  • Private limited companies (Ltd) and public limited companies (Plc) give shareholders limited liability — they can only lose what they invested.
  • Suitability depends on context — start-ups often begin as sole traders or partnerships and move to Ltd or Plc status as they grow and the risks rise.

lessons.title: Business Aims & Objectives
lessons.description: Profit, survival, growth, service and market share — why businesses set objectives, how they differ and change.
lessons.content_html:
Aims vs Objectives

An aim is the big-picture destination — where the business wants to end up. An objective is a specific, measurable target that moves the business closer to the aim. If Costa Coffee’s aim is to be the UK’s leading coffee chain, one of its objectives might be to open 50 new stores this year. Aims tell you the destination; objectives tell you the route. Good objectives are usually SMART — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

The Main Objectives Businesses Set

The specification names five common objectives: profit, survival, growth, providing a service, and market share. The first, and often the only one for a brand-new business, is survival — just keeping the lights on through the fragile early months. Once past that, most businesses aim for profit, making enough revenue over costs that the owners are rewarded for their work and risk. Growth, measured by sales, employees or by opening new sites, is another common goal — Greggs has grown from a Newcastle bakery to over 2,500 UK shops.

Market share targets focus on taking sales from rivals. Providing a service — supplying something customers genuinely need at a reliable standard — is the main objective for public-service organisations like the NHS, for charities, and for some private firms that market themselves on quality rather than cheap price. John Lewis historically pitched itself on service over price; Apple does the same.

Key Fact

The main objectives businesses set are profit, survival, growth, providing a service, and market share. Different objectives suit different stages of the business and different types of organisation.

Why Set Objectives at All?

Objectives give a business direction. Without them, staff pull in different directions and decisions are made reactively rather than strategically. Clear objectives motivate workers — a target to open five new stores by December gives everyone something concrete to aim at. They provide a yardstick for measuring success: did the business hit a 15% market share or not? They support planning because without a target, you cannot decide how much money, staff or stock you need. Finally, they help a business secure finance — banks and investors want evidence the business knows where it is going before they lend. Without clear objectives, a business also struggles to prioritise: when cash is tight, which project gets cut first? Objectives answer that question before the pressure hits.

Why Different Businesses Have Different Objectives

The specification explicitly asks why different businesses have different objectives. Three contrasting examples make the point. A sole trader setting up a freelance photography business in her first year will prioritise survival and a modest profit — she needs enough income to pay rent and buy kit, not global growth. A Plc like Unilever has survived the early stages and operates in dozens of countries, so it focuses on growth (new markets, new product ranges), market share (against Nestlé and Procter & Gamble) and shareholder returns. A charity like Oxfam drops profit entirely and sets service objectives — number of families supplied with clean water, number of schools rebuilt after a disaster. Oxfam’s success is not measured in pounds of profit but in people served.

The size of the business, the stage it is at, whether it is for-profit or not-for-profit, and the level of competition all shape the objective mix. The same decision — say, whether to cut prices — is right or wrong depending on whether the objective is market share, service quality or short-term profit.

A start-up’s priority is survival — profit can wait until customers and cash flow are stable. A multinational like Unilever has survived the early phase, so it focuses on growth, market share and shareholder returns. A not-for-profit like Oxfam drops profit altogether and sets service objectives (e.g. number of clean-water projects delivered). The level of competition also matters — in a crowded market like streaming, Netflix must fight to hold market share; in a niche market, providing a high-quality service may be enough.

Why Objectives Change as Businesses Evolve

Objectives evolve with the business. In its first year, a street-food start-up like a new burger van focuses on survival — cover costs, build a regular customer base. As it settles, it may target profit. If a second van follows, the focus shifts to growth. An established business like Tesco now talks heavily about sustainability and reducing plastic — service and reputation rise up the agenda once the basics are secure. Objectives can also change in response to external events: during the 2023 cost-of-living squeeze, many retailers quietly dropped ambitious growth targets and returned to survival and customer retention.

Key Fact

A business’s objectives typically change as it grows — from survival in year one, to profit and growth as it stabilises, and to service or market share once it is established. The same business may hold several objectives at once.

Yes — and this is where strong evaluation answers come from. Profit pushes businesses to cut costs; a service objective pushes them to maintain quality even when it is expensive. Growth can damage service quality if expansion runs ahead of training. Market share fights (heavy discounting) can damage profit in the short term. A good answer names the tension and weighs it — e.g. ‘aggressive growth might hit short-term profit because of the cost of new stores, but in the long term it locks in market share that protects future profit.’
lessons.exam_tip_html: When questions ask you to recommend objectives, match the objective to the stage and type of business in the case study. A brand-new cafe does not need market share as its main objective; a Plc does not need survival. Watch for the word ‘most important’ in 12-mark statements — your conclusion must introduce a new weighting, not just repeat points already made. Avoid the common trap of writing about objectives in the abstract — always anchor your answer to the named business.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Objectives are SMART targets that turn a business’s aim into a measurable plan — they motivate staff, guide planning and help secure finance.
  • The main objectives are profit, survival, growth, providing a service, and market share.
  • Different businesses set different objectives, and the same business’s objectives change over time as size, stage and competition shift.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether profit should always be the most important objective for a UK private limited company. Arguments against profit as main objective: FairBean’s purpose is the fair-trade mission; a service objective is consistent with that mission and is what customers pay a premium for; prioritising short-term profit could undermine the brand’s credibility and drive away ethical consumers. Supported judgement: profit is necessary but not sufficient for FairBean; the right framing is probably that profit is a constraint (must stay in the black) but service to farmers remains the lead objective. [9 marks]

lessons.title: Stakeholders in Business
lessons.description: Who has a stake in a business, how business activity affects them, and how they in turn influence the business.
lessons.content_html:
Who Are Stakeholders?

A stakeholder is anyone who is affected by or has an interest in what a business does. When a new Greggs opens in a town, the impact spreads far wider than the bakery itself — owners expect profit, staff gain jobs, customers get sausage rolls, rival coffee shops lose trade, suppliers win a new contract, the local community gets extra footfall, and the government gains tax on every sale. Each of these groups has a different ‘stake’ in the decision.

The specification splits stakeholders into two groups. Internal stakeholders work inside the business: owners, managers and employees. External stakeholders are outside but still affected: customers, suppliers, the local community and the government. Every big decision helps some and hurts others — and those who are hurt will push back.

The Main Stakeholder Groups and Their Objectives

Owners (sole traders, partners or shareholders) invest their money and time. They want profits, dividends and a rising share value. Employees depend on the business for their pay and security. They want high wages, job security, safe conditions and the chance to develop. Customers want quality products at fair prices, honest advertising and reliable after-sales service.

Suppliers want prompt payment and long-term contracts so they can plan their own business. The local community wants jobs and investment, but objects to noise, pollution or traffic — if Amazon opens a new warehouse, locals want the jobs but not the lorries clogging the road at 4am. The government is also a stakeholder: it collects corporation tax, VAT, income tax and employer National Insurance from every UK business, it regulates how businesses operate through consumer, employment and environmental law, and it funds public services that a healthy business base makes possible. Every time a business grows, hires or imports, the government has a stake in the outcome.

Key Fact

Internal stakeholders are owners, managers and employees. External stakeholders are customers, suppliers, local community and government. Each has different, often competing, objectives — the business must balance them to succeed.

The Effect of Business Activity on Stakeholders

Every business decision radiates out to different stakeholders. When Morrisons cuts 150 middle-management jobs, shareholders may cheer the cost savings while the affected employees lose their income and morale drops across the remaining workforce. When a new Aldi opens in a town, customers gain lower prices, but independent grocers nearby may lose enough trade to close. When Tesla opens a Gigafactory, the local community gets thousands of jobs, but also extra traffic and pressure on local housing.

Even an apparently positive decision — raising staff wages, for example — can be divisive: employees welcome the rise, owners see profits dip, and customers face higher prices as costs are passed on. Suppliers caught in the pay squeeze may lose orders if the business stops buying to protect margins. The government is affected too: a business making larger profits pays more corporation tax; a business closing a factory drops employees onto unemployment benefit, costing the taxpayer. Good managers ask, before every major choice, ‘who benefits, who pays, and how loudly will the losers object?’ A decision that ignores this question rarely survives contact with reality.

Imagine a delivery firm decides to switch to 24-hour operations. Owners benefit — higher revenue and better use of vans. Customers benefit — overnight deliveries. Employees split: some welcome the night-shift premium, others hate the hours. Suppliers near the depot must also work later. The local community loses — sleep-disturbing lorry noise at 3am. The local council (government) fields complaints and may tighten planning conditions. This is stakeholder conflict: one decision, multiple opposing reactions. The business cannot please everyone, so it must judge which group matters most to its success.

The Effect of Stakeholders on the Business

Stakeholders are not passive — they have levers they can pull. Owners and shareholders can vote at annual general meetings, replace directors or refuse further investment. Employees can work harder, strike, quit, or go slow — poor treatment kills productivity. Customers vote with their wallets: when Boohoo was linked to underpaid factory workers in Leicester, sales fell and the share price halved within days. Suppliers can demand upfront payment or refuse to extend credit when a firm becomes risky.

The local community can block planning applications or run a campaign through the local media. The government influences businesses through tax rates (higher corporation tax lowers retained profit), regulation (consumer law, minimum wage, environmental rules), and government spending (decisions to contract NHS services can make or break a supplier). Different stakeholders carry different weight. A Tesco Plc decision is shaped heavily by big shareholders, while a village cafe lives or dies on the goodwill of its local community. The shift from private to public ownership often means managers now spend more time managing investor expectations than they do serving customers.

Key Fact

Stakeholder objectives often conflict: owners want dividends, employees want higher pay, customers want lower prices, the local community wants minimal disruption and the government wants tax and law-compliance. A business cannot maximise all at once — managing the trade-offs is a core leadership skill.

Businesses resolve conflicts through trade-offs and communication. A factory can invest in quieter machinery to reduce community complaints while preserving production. A supermarket can introduce self-checkouts (cuts costs, helps shareholders) but redeploy staff into personal shopping roles rather than making them redundant. Clear communication — explaining a decision honestly — often softens the blow even when the decision itself is unpopular. The businesses that survive conflict best are those that treat stakeholders as partners rather than obstacles.
lessons.exam_tip_html: OCR splits stakeholder questions into two directions — the effect OF business activity on stakeholders AND the effect OF stakeholders on the business. Check which direction the question is asking about before you start writing. For Analyse questions, pick one group and develop the chain of reasoning rather than listing all stakeholders superficially. A good answer reads: ‘Employees depend on the business for pay — a round of redundancies cuts their income, which lowers spending power locally, which damages morale for those who remain and increases staff turnover, raising recruitment costs for the business.’
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stakeholders are internal (owners, managers, employees) or external (customers, suppliers, local community, government) — each has different objectives that often conflict.
  • Business activity affects stakeholders: a single decision can raise profits for owners while costing jobs or disturbing neighbours.
  • Stakeholders also affect the business — through purchases, strikes, planning objections, regulation and tax — so managing stakeholder relationships protects long-term success.

Which one of the following is an external stakeholder?
A) An employee of the business
B) A customer
C) A manager
D) An owner
practice_questions.marks:
B) A customer [1 mark]
External stakeholders sit outside the business. Customers, suppliers, the local community and the government are external. Employees, managers and owners are internal. Attempt every MCQ — blank answers score zero.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way in which the government is a stakeholder in a UK business.

practice_questions.text: Outline one way a decision to close a local factory might affect the local community. (Context: a food-processing firm in a small Cumbrian town announces it will shut its main factory, which employs 180 local people.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a relevant effect (e.g. unemployment rises, local spending falls, nearby shops lose customers, house prices drop).
2 marks: adds development with application to the Cumbrian town — e.g. ‘180 local people will lose their jobs (1), cutting household spending at local shops and pubs and lowering the whole town’s economic activity (1).’
One-word answers score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way customers can influence the decisions of a business they disapprove of. (Context: in 2020 newspaper reports linked the fast-fashion retailer Boohoo to underpaid garment workers in Leicester.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies that customers can switch away or boycott (AO1).
2 marks: applies to Boohoo — e.g. shoppers stopping purchases after the news (AO2).
3 marks: develops the consequence — sales fell, the share price halved, and the business had to publicly investigate its supply chain to win customers back.
Indicative answer: ‘Customers can influence a business by choosing to spend their money elsewhere (1). When news stories linked Boohoo to underpaid workers in Leicester, many shoppers switched to rivals (2), cutting Boohoo’s sales and halving its share price, which forced the business to publicly investigate its supply chain to regain customer trust (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how stakeholder conflict might arise when a UK business decides to switch to 24-hour operations. (Context: RapidParcel, a logistics firm based near a residential area in Birmingham, is planning to move to round-the-clock lorry movements from its depot.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning anchored to RapidParcel. Chain 1: owners and customers benefit from 24-hour operations → higher revenue, faster delivery service → profits and service objective both supported. Chain 2: local community (external) and some employees (internal) lose → 3am lorry noise disturbs residents → planning objections or council restrictions → named consequence for RapidParcel (e.g. council tightens operating hours, forcing the firm to run a partial service overnight). Shows the two-way effect.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear application to RapidParcel, at least one reaching a named consequence.
Developing: Chain started but loosely applied.
Emerging: Lists stakeholders without building a chain, no application to the case. A generic answer cannot score above 3. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Recommend one action a business could take to manage stakeholder conflict when opening a new facility in a residential area. Justify your recommendation. (Context: SunBake Ltd is planning a new bakery on the edge of a quiet residential village in Kent. It will employ 40 people but will need 4am flour deliveries.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument that considers multiple stakeholder groups (local community, employees, owners, council/government), applied to SunBake, with a clear recommendation that weights the most important factor. Examples of recommended actions: investing in quieter delivery vehicles; shifting delivery to 6am; holding a community consultation; hiring locally; sponsoring local amenities.
Secure: Developed arguments, clear recommendation, some application to SunBake.
Developing: Some points made, limited development, recommendation restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported recommendation.

Key tensions to weigh: local community vs owners (noise vs profit); employees (welcome the jobs) vs community (unwelcome disruption); council as regulator (planning permission depends on community satisfaction).
Supported recommendation: a strong answer identifies that community goodwill is critical because SunBake needs the council’s planning permission AND local staff AND local customers — so measures that directly address community concerns (later delivery time, quieter vehicles, visible community investment) outweigh pure profit maximisation in the opening months. [12 marks]

lessons.title: Business Growth
lessons.description: Organic vs external growth — mergers, takeovers and horizontal, vertical or diversification.
lessons.content_html:
Why Businesses Grow

Once a business is stable, the owners usually want it to grow. Business growth can mean selling to more customers, opening in new regions, launching new products or buying another firm outright. The rewards can be huge — bigger profits, a stronger brand and more influence over suppliers — but growth also brings extra risk, extra cost and more complicated decisions. The OCR specification splits growth into two clear routes: growth from the inside out (organic) and growth from the outside in (external).

Organic Growth

Organic growth is growth a business generates under its own steam. The OCR spec names four routes: increasing output, gaining new customers, developing new products and increasing market share. Greggs is the textbook UK example — it has grown from a single Newcastle shop in 1951 to more than 2,500 bakeries across the country, one lease and one shop team at a time. No mergers, no takeovers. The business put profits back into opening the next branch.

Increasing output means making and selling more of what you already do. JD Wetherspoon raised output by opening longer hours and serving breakfast. Gaining new customers means reaching people who do not yet buy from you — Gymshark did this by posting workout content on Instagram rather than paying for traditional adverts, pulling in gym-goers worldwide. Developing new products widens what the business offers — Tesla added a home battery (Powerwall) to its electric car range. Increasing market share means winning sales from rivals — Aldi has steadily taken grocery share from Tesco, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons since arriving in the UK in 1990.

Key Fact

Organic growth has four routes in the specification: increasing output, gaining new customers, developing new products and increasing market share. The business funds each step itself, usually from retained profit or a loan.

External Growth

External growth is growth by joining with or buying another business. It is faster than organic growth because the customers, staff, suppliers and shops come with the deal. But it is also riskier — many deals overpay, clash cultures or strip out the very thing that made the target valuable. The OCR spec names two methods: mergers and takeovers.

A merger is an agreement between two firms of roughly equal size to combine into one new business. The 2010 merger of Orange and T-Mobile created EE, which eventually became the UK’s largest mobile network before BT bought it. A takeover is when one firm buys another outright. Morrisons’ takeover of Safeway in 2005 instantly doubled its store count; Amazon’s takeover of Whole Foods in 2017 gave it a physical supermarket chain overnight.

Three Types of External Growth

External growth can happen in three different directions. Each has a different impact on the market and on the business.

Horizontal integration — joining with a rival at the same stage of production. Two rival supermarkets, say Sainsbury’s buying Asda, would be horizontal. It cuts competition and grows market share quickly, but competition regulators (the CMA in the UK) can block deals they think hurt shoppers — which is exactly what happened to the real Sainsbury’s–Asda bid in 2019.

Vertical integration — joining with a business at a different stage of the supply chain. A supermarket buying a farm (backward vertical) controls its own meat and vegetable supply. A farm buying a supermarket chain (forward vertical) controls how its produce reaches shoppers. Vertical deals improve reliability and can cut costs, but bring the business into a part of the supply chain it may not know well.

Diversification — joining with a business in a totally different market. A supermarket buying a bank would be diversification. Tesco Bank is a real UK example — it gave Tesco a way to earn money outside groceries and spread its risk. The drawback is that the new business is unfamiliar territory, and managing something you do not understand often goes wrong.

Why Choose One Over the Other?

The choice between organic and external growth depends on how fast the business wants to grow, how much money it can afford to commit, and how much risk the owners are prepared to carry. Organic growth is cheaper and lower-risk — but it is slow and may let rivals move first. External growth is fast and can transform a business overnight — but takeovers often fail because the firms cannot merge their cultures, or because the buyer paid too much.

Reasons for growth matter too. The spec highlights that firms grow to reach more customers, to raise profit, to build a stronger brand, and to gain power over suppliers and rivals. But bigger is not always better — a rapid takeover can damage staff morale if jobs are cut, and customers can lose out if competition disappears. A good answer weighs both sides rather than assuming growth is always a good thing.

Key Fact

The three types of external growth are horizontal (joining a rival at the same stage), vertical (joining a supplier or distributor) and diversification (joining a business in a totally different market). Each changes the shape of the combined firm differently.

Growth usually means higher revenue and a bigger brand, but it also brings pressure. Communication gets harder when hundreds of staff are scattered across the country. Decisions slow down as more managers have to sign off. Customers may feel the service is less personal. A good answer in the exam recognises that growth is a balance of gains and losses — and that the right choice depends on the business in the case study.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to classify a deal as horizontal, vertical or diversification, look carefully at what each business does. Two firms at the same stage = horizontal; different stages of the supply chain = vertical; unrelated markets = diversification. For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, build a chain of reasoning: the type of growth → how it changes the market → a named impact on the business in the case study. For 9-mark ‘Discuss’ or 12-mark ‘Evaluate/Recommend’ answers, always weigh one method of growth against another and close with a supported judgement — unsupported conclusions score nothing.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Organic growth is funded internally through more output, new customers, new products and rising market share — slower but safer.
  • External growth comes from mergers (equals joining) and takeovers (one firm buys another) — faster but more expensive and often higher risk.
  • Horizontal (rival), vertical (supply chain) and diversification (different market) describe the direction of external growth and change the combined business differently.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of organic growth?
A) A supermarket buying a rival supermarket chain
B) Two banks agreeing to merge
C) A coffee chain opening a new branch using retained profit
D) A car maker taking over a tyre manufacturer
practice_questions.marks:
C) A coffee chain opening a new branch using retained profit [1 mark]
Organic growth is funded internally without merging with or buying another business. Options A, B and D all describe external growth.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of external growth named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: merger, takeover. Accept also: horizontal, vertical, diversification (as types of merger/takeover direction). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way in which a supermarket could grow organically. (Context: a mid-sized UK supermarket chain based in the North West wants to grow without buying any other businesses.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a named route to organic growth (e.g. increasing output, gaining new customers, developing new products, or increasing market share).
2 marks: adds brief development AND applies to the supermarket scenario.
Indicative answer: ‘The supermarket could develop new own-label products (1) such as a plant-based range, attracting vegan shoppers in the North West without needing to buy a rival chain (1).’ [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business might choose external growth rather than organic growth.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. speed, instant market share, access to expertise, reducing competition).
2 marks: develops the reason logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked point, often a consequence for the business.
Indicative answer: ‘External growth is much faster than organic growth (1), because buying a rival brings the customers, stores and staff in a single deal rather than opening new shops one at a time (2). This lets the business reach a target size in months rather than years, which matters when a rival might otherwise beat them to the market (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket of taking over a farm that supplies its vegetables. (Context: a large UK supermarket has just agreed a £90 million deal to buy a chain of farms in Lincolnshire.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from the vertical takeover and end with named, applied consequences for the supermarket. Sustained use of the scenario (Lincolnshire farms, £90m, vegetable supply) throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains with clear cause-effect linkage and some application.
Developing: One chain developed, limited application to the scenario.
Emerging: Simple points with little development or scenario use.
Indicative content:
- Control over supply → more reliable vegetable stock on shelves → fewer gaps → better customer experience, protecting market share in competitive grocery sector.
- Backward vertical integration → cuts the middle-man margin → lower unit cost of vegetables → the supermarket can hold prices down against rivals like Aldi or Lidl.
Counterweights candidates may credit: £90m deal is a sunk cost that cannot be undone if consumer demand falls; farming is a new industry with unfamiliar risks (weather, disease, land regulation). [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a fast-growing UK craft brewery should grow organically or by taking over a smaller rival. (Context: a craft brewery founded in Leeds in 2018 has grown to 40 staff and is now choosing between (A) building a second brewery from scratch in Manchester or (B) buying a smaller independent brewery in Liverpool that has an established customer base but outdated kit.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments on both options applied directly to the craft brewery. Supported judgement that weighs one factor as most important (e.g. speed vs control) or uses an ‘it depends on X’ framing with X justified.
Secure: Developed arguments on both sides, clear recommendation, some application.
Developing: Some points on both sides with limited development; conclusion restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported judgement.

Arguments for organic (A): full control over the new site, no overpayment risk, brand consistency protected, lower upfront cost, builds in-house team capability.
Arguments for takeover (B): instant customer base in Liverpool, quicker route into a new city, existing staff who know local pubs and tastes, faster growth to fight off bigger craft brands.
Against organic: slower, may miss market window, Manchester build could overrun on cost.
Against takeover: outdated kit in Liverpool needs replacing, culture clash between Leeds founders and Liverpool staff, risk of overpaying.
Judgement: credit students who note the decision depends on how fast rivals are expanding and whether the brewery’s cash can absorb the takeover price. Unsupported judgements (‘I think option A is better’) cap below the top band. [12 marks]

lessons.title: Role & Purpose of Marketing
lessons.description: What marketing does — identifying customers, understanding needs, informing them and driving sales.
lessons.content_html:
What Marketing Really Does

Most people hear ‘marketing’ and picture adverts. Adverts are part of it — but they are the last step, not the whole job. Marketing is everything a business does to work out who its customers are, what they want, and how to persuade them to buy. The OCR specification sets out four outcomes that marketing must achieve: identifying customers, understanding them, informing them, and increasing sales.

Think about Gymshark. The founder, Ben Francis, started in a Birmingham garage in 2012. He did not begin with an advert. He began by working out who his customer was — young gym-goers who wanted fitted, stylish training clothes rather than baggy football shirts. He understood them by spending hours in gyms and on Instagram, listening to what they actually said. Only then did he inform them — through fitness influencers, not TV — and drive sales that grew from zero to more than a billion pounds in a decade. Each stage of marketing fed the next.

The Four Purposes of Marketing

The OCR spec names four things marketing must do. Every later marketing lesson — research, segmentation, the 4Ps — flows back to these four outcomes.

Identifying customers — working out who will buy the product. No business can please everyone, so it picks a target group first. LEGO identifies children aged 4–11 and their parents; Saga identifies over-50s; Aldi identifies price-conscious shoppers. Getting this wrong is the most expensive mistake a business can make — if the product is not for anyone specific, nobody will feel it is for them.

Understanding customers — once identified, the business has to learn what these customers actually need. Tesco does this through its Clubcard, which logs what millions of shoppers buy week by week. Small firms do it by talking to customers at the counter. Either way, the aim is the same: replace guesswork with evidence.

Informing customers — once the business knows the customer and the product fits, customers need to hear about it. This is where adverts, social media, shop windows and packaging come in. Monzo informed new customers mainly through word of mouth and a sharp orange card that looked different to every other UK bank card — cheaper than TV ads and far more memorable.

Increasing sales — the first three purposes only matter if customers actually buy. Marketing drives sales by matching the right product to the right customer at the right price in the right place — the four Ps we study in later lessons. Successful marketing turns interest into revenue.

Key Fact

The four purposes of marketing in the specification are: identifying customers, understanding customers, informing customers, and increasing sales. Every marketing decision a business makes should connect back to one of these four outcomes.

Why Identifying Customers Comes First

Before a business designs a product, sets a price or books an advert, it has to answer one question: who is the customer? Get that wrong and everything else — price, packaging, shops, adverts — misses the target. Research and development, manufacturing, packaging and launch adverts all cost money, and a product that nobody wants wastes every pound of it.

That is why identifying the customer is the first step in marketing. It reduces risk. The business commits cash only to products the market actually wants. A start-up selling vegan sports drinks in a rural farming town is less likely to succeed than one selling them in central London — not because the product is bad, but because the customer base is different. Identifying the right customer in the right place is the start of every good marketing plan.

Why Understanding Customers Matters

Identifying the customer is only half the job. The business also has to understand them deeply — their habits, their budgets, their values, the other products they already use. Greggs spotted that an older, lunchtime-focused customer base was shifting towards younger office workers looking for healthier and plant-based options. That understanding led to the vegan sausage roll in 2019 — a product that became one of Greggs’ best-selling lines and repositioned the brand for a younger crowd.

Understanding customers also feeds directly into the marketing mix. Once you know the customer, you can decide what the product should look like, what price they will pay, where they shop, and which adverts they will actually see. A business that skips this step guesses — and usually loses.

Marketing Drives Sales

The final purpose of marketing is also the one that keeps a business alive: revenue from sales. Without sales there is no business. Marketing does not replace a good product — if the product is poor, no amount of marketing saves it — but it does amplify a good one. A brilliant product no customers know about will fail; a good product matched to the right audience at the right price will sell.

The four purposes therefore sit in a chain: identify → understand → inform → sell. Break any link and sales suffer. A business that informs customers about a product they do not need loses the advertising cost for nothing. A business that understands its customers but never tells them about a new product misses the sales opportunity entirely. Good marketing strings all four together.

Key Fact

Marketing fails when any of the four purposes is skipped. Identifying without understanding leads to products nobody wants. Understanding without informing leads to great products nobody has heard of. Informing without identifying wastes money telling the wrong people.

Large firms can afford dedicated marketing teams, expensive research panels and national TV campaigns. Tesco spends over £300 million a year on marketing. A small independent bakery cannot match that — but it does not need to. It can identify customers by chatting over the counter, understand them by remembering their usual order, inform them through a local Instagram account and increase sales through loyalty cards and word of mouth. The four purposes apply to every business; the scale just changes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark ‘Explain’ questions on the role of marketing, always apply to the business in the case study — a generic answer loses the application mark. For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, build a chain of reasoning that links one marketing purpose (e.g. understanding customers) to a named business outcome (a better product, higher sales, less wasted advertising spend). A common mistake is to describe ‘marketing’ only as advertising — examiners look for candidates who see identifying, understanding, informing and sales as connected stages.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four purposes of marketing are identifying customers, understanding them, informing them and increasing sales — each feeds the next.
  • Identifying the customer first reduces risk; understanding them replaces guesswork with evidence before the business commits cash.
  • Every marketing decision — product, price, promotion, place — should trace back to one of the four purposes. If it does not, the business is spending money for no clear reason.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the role of marketing?
A) Producing goods as cheaply as possible
B) Keeping accurate financial records
C) Identifying customers and meeting their needs to increase sales
D) Training staff to use new machinery
practice_questions.marks:
C) Identifying customers and meeting their needs to increase sales [1 mark]
Marketing is about customers, not production, finance or training. Options A, B and D describe operations, finance and HR.

practice_questions.text: State one purpose of marketing named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: identifying customers, understanding customers, informing customers, increasing sales. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one reason why a business needs to understand its customers. (Context: a small UK bakery chain is planning to launch a new range of pastries.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. to design the right product, to avoid wasted spending, to stay ahead of rivals).
2 marks: adds brief development AND applies to the bakery.
Indicative answer: ‘Understanding customers helps the bakery choose flavours customers actually want (1), avoiding the cost of baking pastries that sit unsold (1).’ [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which marketing can help a business to increase sales. (Context: an independent coffee shop in Bristol has seen sales flatten over the past year.)
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a way marketing increases sales (e.g. informing customers through social media, launching a new product after research, offering promotions).
2 marks: develops the point logically.
3 marks: adds a second linked development applied to the Bristol coffee shop.
Indicative answer: ‘The shop could use social media to inform local customers about a new seasonal drink (1). This reaches a wider audience than relying on walk-by foot traffic alone (2), which should pull new students and young workers into the shop and lift sales again (3).’ [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how identifying its customers helps a new UK business. (Context: a Leeds-based start-up is launching a range of plant-based ready meals aimed at health-conscious students.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from identifying the target customer (health-conscious Leeds students) and end in a named business outcome. Sustained use of the scenario throughout.
Secure: Two developed chains, clear cause-effect, some application.
Developing: One chain developed; limited application.
Emerging: Lists benefits of identifying customers without applying to the scenario.
Indicative chains:
- Identifying the target customer → knows flavours and portion sizes that suit students → product designed to fit student lifestyles → higher sales and less wasted stock.
- Identifying the customer → chooses promotion channels students actually use (TikTok, university Instagram) → cheaper marketing spend → more revenue per pound spent.
Application hooks the scenario offers: Leeds, students, plant-based, health-conscious, ready meal format. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the importance of the four purposes of marketing for a new small UK business. (Context: two friends are opening a new vegan cafe in a busy university city and only have £12,000 to spend on their launch.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Developed arguments on why each purpose matters, balanced against limits and trade-offs, applied throughout to the vegan cafe and the £12,000 budget. Supported judgement on which purposes matter most.
Secure: Developed arguments on most purposes with some application and a clear judgement.

lessons.title: Market Research
lessons.description: Primary vs secondary research, qualitative vs quantitative data — and picking the right method.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Market Research?

Market research is how a business finds out what customers want, what rivals are doing and how big the market really is. Without it, decisions are guesswork. With it, a business can launch products, set prices and design adverts based on evidence from real people and real data. The specification requires you to know how different methods and sources of research suit different business questions — and how to use both qualitative and quantitative data.

Tesco is a useful example. Its Clubcard scheme collects data from millions of shoppers every week, telling Tesco which products are selling, which adverts worked and where to open the next store. A small independent bakery cannot match that scale, but it can still do good research — a ten-minute walk around the high street to count rivals is research; a short chat at the counter about what customers would try next is research. Research does not have to be expensive; it has to answer the business question.

Key Fact

Market research splits two ways: by WHO collects it (primary = the business itself; secondary = someone else already) and by WHAT kind of data it collects (qualitative = opinions and reasons; quantitative = numbers and measurable facts).

Primary Research Methods

Primary research is brand-new information the business collects for itself. It is gathered for a specific purpose, so it is relevant and up to date — but it takes time and money. The OCR specification names four primary methods: questionnaires, interviews, trialling and focus groups.

Questionnaires — a set of written questions sent online, emailed, posted or handed out. They can reach large samples quickly and the answers are easy to count, but written questions cannot probe feelings deeply.

Interviews — a one-to-one conversation between a researcher and a customer. They produce rich, detailed answers, but are slow and expensive, and the interviewer can unintentionally lead the answers.

Trialling — letting a small group use the actual product before launch. Deliveroo did this in Chelsea for six months in 2013 before rolling the app out nationwide. Trialling is powerful because customers react to the real thing, not a description — but it is expensive because the business has to make the product first.

Focus groups — a small group of 6–10 target customers discusses a product while a researcher listens. Honest reactions are captured, but one loud voice can dominate and bias the result.

Secondary Research Sources

Secondary research uses information that already exists — someone else collected it first. It is fast and cheap, but it may be out of date or not quite fit the question. The OCR spec names four secondary sources: newspapers and magazines, the census, websites, and internal data.

Newspapers and magazines carry articles on market trends, rival launches and industry reports — useful for spotting the competitive landscape. The census, carried out every ten years by the Office for National Statistics, shows the age, income and location of the UK population in detail — ideal for picking a target segment. Websites include competitor sites, review platforms like Trustpilot, government data and market reports from firms like Mintel; most are free or cheap.

Internal data is the goldmine most small businesses forget about — information the business already has from its own systems. EPOS till data shows which products sell best and at what times. Customer databases record repeat buying, email open rates and average order values. Loyalty card schemes join all this together. Internal data is free, specific to the business and always up to date.

Qualitative vs Quantitative Data

Qualitative data gathers opinions, feelings and reasons — why customers buy, how they feel about a brand. Interviews and focus groups produce qualitative data. It is rich and detailed but hard to turn into a graph.

Quantitative data records numbers — how many people, how much they spend, how often they buy. Large-scale questionnaires, till data and census figures produce quantitative data. It is easy to plot on charts and compare across segments, but it does not explain why.

Good businesses use both. Tesco’s Clubcard shows what customers buy (quantitative); a focus group then explains why they switched from Tesco to Aldi (qualitative). Together, the two answer the full question. Netflix does the same thing — its servers log which shows are watched and for how long (quantitative), while surveys explore why people cancel their subscription (qualitative). A decision worth hundreds of millions of pounds needs more than one angle.

Matching the Method to the Question

Which method a business picks depends on the question, the budget and the time available. A brand-new start-up with £500 cannot afford focus groups run by a research agency; it can afford a free online survey shared on Instagram. A big supermarket trialling a new ready meal can trial it in ten stores first, cheaply gathering real sales data before a national rollout. Picking the wrong method wastes money — running a focus group to find out how many people shop at a supermarket is using an expensive qualitative tool to answer a quantitative question.

Research is never perfect. Sample size matters — a survey of 30 people is too small to trust. Sampling bias distorts the result — asking shoppers outside Waitrose will not tell you what Aldi shoppers think. Leading questions (‘don’t you agree our product is great?’) push customers to answer the way the business hoped. And customers sometimes say what sounds good rather than what they will actually do, especially on price or ethics. A business that does not check these issues can make a very costly decision based on flawed data.

Market Size and Market Share

Market research also produces the data behind two key numbers. Market size is the total value or volume of sales in a market — the UK coffee shop market, for instance, is worth around £5 billion per year. Market share is the slice of that market one business controls. The formula is: market share (%) = (business sales ÷ total market sales) × 100. If Costa’s UK coffee sales are £1.1 billion and the total coffee shop market is £5 billion, Costa’s market share is (1.1 ÷ 5) × 100 = 22%. Tracking market share over time is more useful than tracking sales alone — if Costa’s sales rise 3% but the whole market grows 10%, Costa is actually losing ground to Pret and Caffè Nero.

Key Fact

Market share (%) = (business sales ÷ total market sales) × 100. A change in market share is more revealing than a change in sales on its own, because it shows how the business is doing compared with rivals.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to pick the ‘best method’ of research, explain why it suits the specific business in the case study — a small start-up cannot afford nationwide focus groups, while a big brand like Cadbury can. For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, link the research method to a decision the business then makes (e.g. EPOS till data → reveals sales drop among over-50s → launches new advert aimed at that segment). For calculations like market share, always show working and include the % sign — examiners credit method marks even if the final number is wrong.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary research (questionnaires, interviews, trialling, focus groups) is new and tailored; secondary research (newspapers, the census, websites, internal data) is fast and cheap but may be out of date.
  • Qualitative data explains why through opinions; quantitative data tells you how many through numbers — businesses use both together.
  • Market size is total sales in a market; market share = (business sales ÷ total market sales) × 100, and tracks how a business is doing compared with rivals.
