lessons.title: Market Segmentation
lessons.description: Splitting markets by age, gender, income, location and lifestyle to target the right customers.
lessons.content_html:
Why Split the Market?

No business can please everyone. A supermarket that tries to be the cheapest, the most luxurious, the most ethical and the most convenient at the same time ends up being none of them. That is why businesses use market segmentation — they split the whole market into smaller groups of customers who share similar characteristics, pick one or more groups to focus on, and design the product, price, promotion and place to match that group exactly. The OCR specification names five ways to segment: age, gender, income, location and lifestyle.

Targeting is the next step. Once a business has split the market into segments, it chooses which segment or segments to serve. Aldi targets price-conscious shoppers; Waitrose targets high-income households who want quality and service. Both are supermarkets; both are successful; they simply picked different segments.

Key Fact

The five segmentation bases in the OCR specification are age, gender, income, location and lifestyle. Each lets a business design a marketing mix aimed at one specific group rather than wasting money trying to please everyone.

The Five Bases in Detail

Age — splitting the market into age bands. LEGO targets children aged 4–11, Netflix teen comedies target 13–19, and Saga holidays and insurance target the over-50s. Each age group has different spending power, different interests and different media habits. An advert that works on TikTok for a 17-year-old rarely works for a 70-year-old.

Gender — splitting by male, female or non-binary customers. Fragrance brands like Lynx design products around young male shoppers, while Dove’s ‘Real Beauty’ campaigns target women. Sports brands often launch separate lines too — Gymshark’s womenswear range now matches its menswear in size.

Income — splitting by how much customers earn. Aldi and Lidl target shoppers who want the lowest price. Waitrose and Fortnum & Mason target higher-income households who will pay more for quality and service. Income segmentation shapes price, product quality and where the shops open — Aldi moves into areas with lower average incomes, Waitrose into wealthier commuter towns.

Location — splitting by where customers live. A surf shop in Newquay stocks very different products to a ski shop in Aviemore, even though both sell sports gear. Location affects weather, culture, language and which rivals are nearby. Greggs runs different offers in the north and south of England to reflect regional tastes.

Lifestyle — splitting by how customers live: active or sedentary, health-conscious or indulgent, outdoorsy, vegan, luxury-focused. Gymshark targets young fitness enthusiasts who train regularly and post workout content online; The North Face targets the outdoorsy segment who hike, climb and ski. Lifestyle is the newest of the five bases and overlaps with age and income, but it is powerful because it captures how people spend their time and money, not just their demographics.

Segmentation in Action — Aldi vs Waitrose

Aldi and Waitrose sell the same basic goods — bread, milk, vegetables — but their segmentation is completely different. Aldi targets income (low to mid), location (everywhere, including smaller towns) and lifestyle (value-seeking, practical). Its stores are no-frills, its own-brand products sit on pallets, and its adverts use the slogan ‘Like brands, only cheaper’.

Waitrose targets income (high), location (commuter towns and wealthier city suburbs) and lifestyle (quality-focused, ethically minded, time-rich). Its stores feel premium, its adverts focus on British farming and sourcing, and prices are noticeably higher. Neither supermarket is trying to win the other’s customers — both have designed their whole marketing mix around a different segment and are happy to stay there.

Segmentation in Action — Gymshark and Saga

Gymshark is built around age (16–25), gender (male and female, with separate ranges), and lifestyle (active, social-media-fluent, gym-focused). The brand rose from a Solihull garage in 2012 to more than a billion pounds in valuation by 2024 — not by trying to sell to every shopper, but by owning one tight segment.

Saga sits at the opposite end of the age axis. It targets the over-50s with insurance, holidays, magazines and cruises. Its products are designed around older customers — large print, easy booking, holidays that travel slower — and its adverts run in newspapers and TV channels watched by older audiences, not on TikTok. Again, the segmentation drives every part of the marketing mix.

Combining Bases

Most larger UK businesses use more than one segmentation base at the same time. Boots divides the health and beauty market by gender (men’s Boots range vs No7 for women), by age (Boots Baby vs Boots 50+ vitamins), by income (premium brands vs own-label) and by location (city-centre flagship stores, retail park ‘beauty’ stores, local pharmacies). Combining bases gives a much sharper picture of the customer than using one base alone — a 55-year-old woman on a high income shopping in central London has different needs to a 20-year-old man on a low income in a market town, even though both are Boots customers. This kind of detail feeds straight into the marketing mix every brand builds.

Key Fact

Segmenting lets a business focus its marketing on people who are likely to buy, which raises the return on every pound spent. Bigger firms usually combine two or more bases (e.g. Boots uses age, gender, income AND location) for a sharper target.

Benefits: marketing spend is focused on people likely to buy, so the return on each pound is higher. Products are designed around real customer needs, raising sales and loyalty. Smaller firms can also compete with giants by owning one segment rather than fighting across the whole market.

Drawbacks: segmentation costs money — the business needs market research to identify segments and may need different products, packaging and adverts for each. There is also a risk of stereotyping customers and missing buyers who do not fit the expected profile. Brands have to watch for segment drift too — when Topshop stopped appealing to its core 16–25 segment, it collapsed into administration in 2021.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark ‘Explain’ questions on segmentation, always apply to the business in the case study — a generic answer loses the application mark. For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, build a chain: the segmentation base → how it changes the marketing mix → a named consequence for the business. A common mistake is to list the five bases without applying them. For 9-mark ‘Discuss’ answers, weigh benefits (focused marketing) against drawbacks (research cost, multiple product lines) before a clear judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five OCR segmentation bases are age, gender, income, location and lifestyle. Each is a different way of splitting customers into groups who share characteristics.
  • Aldi, Waitrose, Gymshark and Saga all succeed because every marketing decision — product, price, shop location, advert — flows from the segment they have chosen.
  • Larger businesses often combine two or more bases for a sharper target — Boots uses age, gender, income and location together across its health and beauty range.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether segmenting customers by lifestyle is more useful than segmenting by age for a new UK streaming service. Emerging: One-sided or unsupported judgement.

Arguments for lifestyle segmentation: captures viewing habits (binge-watchers, sport fans, documentary viewers) which directly shape what shows to buy; more relevant to streaming because two 30-year-olds with different lifestyles want very different content; lets the service position content on social platforms those lifestyles use.
Arguments for age segmentation: easier to measure and target (age is publicly captured in the census and by ad platforms); content ratings are built around age; older and younger viewers differ sharply on price sensitivity and device use.
Drawbacks: lifestyle data is harder and slower to gather than age data, costing more of the £1.5m. Age alone misses the fact that a 70-year-old and a 25-year-old can share the same streaming habits.
Judgement: credit candidates who argue that a combination is strongest — a streaming service should use age for broad channel choice (TikTok for younger, Facebook for older) and lifestyle for content targeting. Pure one-base answers cap below the top band. [12 marks]

lessons.title: Product & the Product Life Cycle
lessons.description: Design, invention, innovation — then tracking products through the four life cycle stages.
lessons.content_html:
The Product Is the Heart of the Marketing Mix

Price, promotion and place all matter — but none of them help if the product itself is wrong. The OCR specification places product at the centre of the marketing mix for a reason. A great advert cannot save a poor product, and a strong product will often sell even with a modest marketing budget. The spec asks you to understand three things about a product before a business even launches it: how it is designed, whether it is truly new (invention) or an improvement (innovation), and how it changes over its life cycle.

Design, Invention and Innovation

Design is where a product begins. Good design balances how the product looks, how it works, what it is made of, and how much it costs to make. Dyson is a British case in point — James Dyson spent five years and more than 5,000 prototypes designing the first bagless vacuum cleaner. The vacuum worked, but it also looked different to every other cleaner on the shelf, which helped it stand out.

There is a useful distinction between invention and innovation. Invention is creating something genuinely new — the first bagless vacuum, the first iPhone, the first electric car. Innovation is improving or adapting what already exists — Apple innovates new iPhone models every year, each better than the last, but none is as new as the original 2007 launch. Most successful UK businesses are innovators rather than inventors, because improving a known product is much less risky than inventing a category customers have never seen.

Design, invention and innovation shape what the product does — which in turn decides the price customers will pay and the promotion needed to sell it. A highly innovative product can charge a premium and justify heavy launch advertising; a mature product may need price cuts to stay competitive.

Key Fact

Invention creates something genuinely new (the first iPhone, Dyson’s bagless vacuum). Innovation improves or adapts what already exists (the iPhone 16, Dyson’s latest cordless model). Most successful UK businesses innovate rather than invent — it is faster, cheaper and safer.

Products Have a Life Cycle

Every product goes through stages over time — it is launched, grows, peaks and eventually declines. The product life cycle (PLC) is the model businesses use to track this journey and decide what to do at each stage. Understanding the cycle stops a business pumping money into a declining product or charging too little for one that is about to take off.

The OCR specification names four stages: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. (You do not need to draw the PLC curve in the exam — the focus is on understanding what happens to sales and profit at each stage, and how the business should respond.)

The Four Stages

Introduction — the product has just launched. Sales grow slowly as customers hear about it for the first time. Prices may be set high (to recover development costs) or low (to pull shoppers away from rivals). Advertising spend is heavy. The business often still makes a loss on the product at this stage. The Nintendo Switch was a classic introduction phase in 2017 — heavy promotion, slow build-up, limited stock.

Growth — sales rise quickly as word spreads and rivals start to react. Profit turns positive as the fixed development costs spread across more units. Tesla’s Model Y has been in growth since launch, with sales climbing each year as more customers choose electric.

Maturity — sales peak and flatten. The market is saturated, competition is fierce, and prices may need to fall to keep customers. The iPhone has been in maturity for several years — annual refreshes keep sales steady rather than booming. At maturity, businesses often respond by refreshing the product (new packaging, new flavours, new features) or cutting the price to hold on to customers.

Decline — sales fall as customers move to newer products. Nokia’s dominance of mobile phones in the 2000s collapsed into decline once Apple and Samsung launched smartphones. At decline, a business must decide whether to withdraw the product, sell it off cheaply, or give it one last refresh.

Key Fact

The four stages of the product life cycle in order are: introduction, growth, maturity and decline. You do not need to draw the PLC curve — you need to say what happens to sales and profit at each stage, and what the business should do in response.

How Businesses Respond at Each Stage

Each stage needs a different response. At introduction, the priority is awareness — heavy advertising and sometimes a big launch event. At growth, the priority is capturing market share before rivals catch up — the business may invest in more production capacity and broader distribution. At maturity, the priority shifts to defending sales — refreshing the product, adjusting the price, rewarding loyal customers. At decline, the business must decide: refresh one more time, sell the product off at a discount, or withdraw it and redirect resources to newer products.

Cadbury’s Dairy Milk has been sold in the UK since 1905 and is a good illustration. Constant product refreshes — Fruit & Nut, Whole Nut, Caramel, Oreo, plant-based versions, limited-edition flavours — have repeatedly pulled it back from the edge of decline and kept it in maturity. Not every product can be saved like this: Blockbuster Video simply could not refresh DVD rental once streaming arrived, and declined into closure by 2013.

Product Differentiation and USPs

Every good product stands out from rivals in some way. A USP (unique selling point) is the feature that gives customers a reason to pick this product over the alternatives. BrewDog’s USP was craft beer with stronger flavour than mainstream UK lagers. Dyson’s USP was bagless cleaning. Tesla’s USP was electric cars that could actually go 300 miles on a charge. A strong USP means the business can charge a higher price and attract loyal customers — and it is far easier to design a USP in at the start than to bolt one on when the product is already in maturity.

Most businesses sell more than one product. Their product portfolio is the full collection. A healthy portfolio has products at different life cycle stages — so as one declines, a younger one is rising to take its place. Apple has the iPhone in maturity (steady profit), the Vision Pro headset in introduction (high spend, low sales), and older iPod models in decline. Balancing the portfolio means the business always has something earning now and something growing for the future.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 3-mark ‘Explain’ questions on the product life cycle, always match the stage to a named business action (introduction → heavy advertising; maturity → refresh or price cut). For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ questions, build a chain: the life cycle stage → the business action → the consequence for the business in the case study. A common mistake is to describe what happens to sales without explaining what the business should do. For 9-mark ‘Discuss’ or 12-mark answers, remember to apply to the specific product and to close with a supported judgement. You do not need to draw the PLC curve.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Every product starts with design, and is either an invention (genuinely new) or an innovation (improvement on something existing).
  • The product life cycle has four stages — introduction, growth, maturity and decline — and each needs a different pricing, promotion and production response.
  • A strong USP lets a business stand out, charge a higher price and build loyal customers — it is far easier to design in at the start than to add later.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how understanding the product life cycle could benefit a UK smartphone business. (Context: a UK smartphone company has an older model that sold well for three years but whose sales have flattened in the past twelve months.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two linked chains of reasoning that start from the product life cycle and end with named, applied consequences for the smartphone business. Sustained scenario use.
Secure: Two developed chains with cause-effect and some application.
Developing: One chain developed; limited application.
Emerging: Lists stages without applying to the scenario.
Indicative chains:
- Recognising that flat sales mean maturity → triggers a product refresh (new features, a cheaper version, bundled accessories) → sales extended for another year → revenue protected while the next model is developed.
- Recognising maturity → business avoids increasing advertising spend wastefully → budget redirected to the next model’s introduction → healthier portfolio, with one product earning and one growing.
Credit candidates who note the risk of misreading the stage — treating a growth product as mature leads to under-investment and missed sales. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether a UK drinks company should invest in a brand-new invention or focus on innovating its existing range. (Context: a UK drinks company already sells a successful range of flavoured waters and is choosing between (A) launching a completely new, protein-enhanced sports drink, or (B) adding three new flavours and updated packaging to the existing flavoured water range.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments on invention (A) and innovation (B), applied directly to the drinks company. Supported judgement that weights one option or uses an ‘it depends on X’ framing with X justified.
Secure: Developed arguments on both options, clear recommendation, some application.
Developing: Some points on both with limited development; conclusion restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided or unsupported judgement.

Arguments for invention (A): higher reward if successful, enters the growing sports drink market, stronger brand story, potential to patent a new formulation, attracts new customers outside the current range.
Arguments for innovation (B): far lower risk (existing flavoured water range is already mature), faster to market, uses existing supply chain and retail relationships, refreshes the range and extends its maturity stage, cheaper to promote because the brand is already known.
Drawbacks: invention needs heavy R&D spend and may flop against established rivals (Lucozade, Powerade); innovation may fail to excite customers if the flavours are not genuinely different.
Judgement: strong candidates argue that innovation (B) is the safer short-term play, while invention (A) may be worth pursuing on the side if the company has the cash reserves. Credit for ‘it depends on cash reserves and competitor activity’ framing with clear support. [12 marks]

lessons.title: Pricing Methods
lessons.description: Cost-plus, competitor, penetration, skimming and promotional pricing — and how to pick one.
lessons.content_html:
Price is the second of the four Ps and it decides two things at once — how much revenue a business earns per sale, and how customers judge the product. Price too high and sales fall; price too low and costs are not covered. This lesson covers the five pricing methods named on the specification and shows how a UK business picks the one that fits.

Cost-Plus Pricing

Cost-plus pricing starts with what it costs to make one unit, then adds a fixed mark-up. A corner bakery that spends 60p making a sausage roll and adds a 100% mark-up sells it at £1.20. A small plumber who fits a new tap — £25 parts, £40 labour cost — might add 30% and charge £84.50. Cost-plus is simple, guarantees a margin on each sale and is fair to justify to customers: ‘this is what it cost us plus a living for us’.

The weakness is that cost-plus ignores what customers will actually pay and what rivals are charging. A competitor selling the same tap fitting at £70 will win the job even if your costs were identical. Cost-plus works best for tradespeople, small manufacturers and menu-based businesses where cost is easy to calculate and competition is limited.

Competitor Pricing

Competitor pricing (sometimes called competitive pricing) sets prices close to rivals. The petrol market is the obvious example — BP, Shell and Tesco garages on the same stretch of road post almost identical pump prices because drivers see the board across the street. Budget airlines like Ryanair and easyJet track each other’s fares hour by hour. Competitor pricing protects market share, but it means the business can never stand out on price alone — it has to differentiate through product, promotion or place.

Key Fact

The five pricing methods on the specification are cost-plus, competitor pricing, penetration pricing, price skimming and promotional pricing. Each one suits different products, markets and objectives.

Penetration Pricing

Penetration pricing launches at a deliberately low price to win customers fast. Aldi and Lidl broke into the UK supermarket market this way in the 1990s and 2000s, undercutting Tesco and Sainsbury’s on everyday items until cost-conscious shoppers tried them and stayed. Streaming services like Disney+ launched at introductory prices well below Netflix to grab early subscribers. Once customers are locked in, prices are nudged up — Disney+ has raised its UK monthly price several times since launch. Penetration works well when a market already has rivals and the new entrant needs visibility.

Price Skimming

Price skimming is the opposite strategy: launch high, aim at early adopters, then cut the price as rivals copy the idea. Apple is the textbook case. A new iPhone launches at its highest UK price — fans queue and pay £1,000+ for the latest model — and within 18 months the price is quietly cut as the next model is prepared. Sony and Microsoft did the same with PlayStation and Xbox launches. Skimming only works when the product genuinely has a USP that early adopters want before anyone else; copy-cat products that try skimming look overpriced and stick on the shelves.

Skimming starts high and works downwards. It suits new, innovative products with a clear USP — early adopters pay a premium for being first. Profit per unit is strong at launch but market share builds slowly. The risk is that rivals copy quickly and the price has to fall faster than planned.

Penetration starts low and works upwards. It suits crowded markets where the new entrant needs visibility — profit per unit is thin at launch but market share builds fast. The risk is that customers used to the low price complain when it rises, and rivals may drop their prices too and wipe out the advantage.

Promotional Pricing

Promotional pricing is a short-term cut to boost sales. It covers several tactics students often see in UK shops: 2-for-1 offers, percentage-off sales, clearance rails and loss leaders. A loss leader is an extreme version — a supermarket selling milk, bread or baked beans at or below cost. The aim is not to profit on the milk but to pull the shopper in, expecting them to fill the trolley with higher-margin items. Boxing Day sales at Next, Black Friday TV deals at Currys and ‘meal deals’ at Tesco and Boots all use promotional pricing to shift stock or raise footfall.

The danger is that customers learn to wait for the next offer and refuse to pay the full price. Iceland’s constant half-price freezer deals trained some shoppers never to buy at the posted price. Promotional pricing works best when it is used occasionally and tied to a clear reason — end of season, new product launch, seasonal event.

Key Fact

Pricing decisions are shaped by costs (the floor), the product’s USP, how crowded the market is and what the business is trying to achieve — survive, grow, maximise profit or defend share.

No single method is ‘best’. A brand-new product with a real innovation can skim; a new entrant in a crowded market needs penetration; a tradesperson needs cost-plus; a supermarket needs a mix of promotional pricing and competitor pricing to defend its weekly shop.

Real businesses often use different methods for different products. Tesco skims its Finest range on launch, competitor-prices its core lines against Asda and Sainsbury’s, and runs promotional pricing on selected items every week. The choice depends on the product, the market, the stage of the product life cycle and the business’s objectives.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Analyse’ and ‘Discuss’ questions, do not just describe the pricing method — link it to the specific business in the case study and build a chain of reasoning (‘which leads to… which means…’). For ‘Recommend’ questions, pick one method clearly, give two developed reasons why it beats an alternative, and tie every reason back to a feature of the business in the scenario. OCR mark schemes specifically state there are no marks for an unsupported judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five OCR pricing methods are cost-plus, competitor, penetration, skimming and promotional — each one fits a different situation.
  • Skimming suits innovative products with a USP; penetration suits new entrants in crowded markets; cost-plus suits simple cost-based sellers.
  • Pricing choice depends on costs, competition, the product life cycle and the objectives of the business.

lessons.title: Promotion & Place
lessons.description: Point of sale, advertising across five channels, plus digital and physical distribution decisions.
lessons.content_html:
Promotion and place are the third and fourth Ps of the marketing mix. Promotion is how a business tells customers about the product; place is how it actually gets the product to them. Even a brilliantly designed product at the right price will fail if nobody knows it exists, or if customers cannot buy it conveniently. This lesson covers both.

What Promotion Is For

Promotion has four jobs: inform, persuade, remind and build brand image. A Cadbury Christmas television advert reminds viewers that Dairy Milk exists, builds warm family associations, and persuades them to pick the purple bar off the shelf in Tesco. A Gymshark Instagram post does the same jobs for a different audience. Different methods suit different products and different customers.

Point of Sale

Point of sale covers any promotion at the place the customer is about to pay. End-of-aisle displays at Tesco, the chocolate bars by the till at WHSmith, the scent of fresh bread near the door of a supermarket, and on-pack stickers that say ‘New’ or ‘50% extra free’ all count. Point-of-sale works because it reaches the customer at the exact moment they are deciding what to buy — it can lift impulse purchases noticeably.

Advertising Across Media

Advertising is paid communication and the OCR spec names five channels.

Television reaches mass audiences with strong images and sound. Premier League football, I’m a Celebrity and the X Factor are used by big UK advertisers like Sky, Aldi and Lidl because millions watch at once. The downside is expense — a single peak-time slot can cost tens of thousands of pounds.

Radio is cheaper and reaches drivers, workers and listeners at breakfast and drive-time. Local stations are useful for local businesses — an independent car garage can advertise on BBC Radio Lancashire at a fraction of the cost of television.

Print media covers newspapers, magazines and leaflets. It targets specific readerships — a luxury watch advert in the Financial Times, a food promotion in Good Housekeeping. Print is declining but still reaches older and niche audiences.

Websites (a business’s own site and paid adverts on sites like Google or the BBC) are highly measurable — every click is tracked. Paid search means a Manchester driving school can appear top of Google when someone types ‘driving lessons Manchester’.

Social media covers Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and X. Gymshark built a billion-pound brand almost entirely through fitness influencers on Instagram and TikTok, at a tiny fraction of what traditional television would have cost. It allows two-way conversation with customers and precise targeting by age, location and interest.

Other Promotional Methods

Alongside point-of-sale and advertising, OCR names price reductions (percentage-off sales, clearance), loss leaders, competitions and free samples. Costa hands out free tasting cups of a new flavour; Lucozade runs Instagram competitions; Next runs a twice-yearly sale; Tesco sells milk at a loss to pull customers in. Each method targets short-term sales without building long-term brand loyalty on its own — so most businesses mix several methods together.

Key Fact

Promotional methods on the specification are point of sale, advertising (TV, radio, print, websites, social media), price reductions, loss leaders, competitions and free samples. Each reaches customers in a different way.

Place — Getting the Product to the Customer

Place is the fourth P. It is every route a product takes from maker to buyer. OCR names two types of route: physical and digital distribution.

Physical Distribution

Physical distribution uses shops. Primark, Greggs, Boots and JD Sports run hundreds of high-street stores across the UK. Customers walk in, see the stock, buy and leave. Physical distribution works best where customers want to see or try before buying (clothes, shoes), for impulse purchases (chocolate, coffee) or where speed matters (a sandwich at lunchtime). The downsides are rent, rates and staff costs.

Digital Distribution

Digital distribution uses websites and apps. ASOS is the UK pioneer — 100% online fashion, no physical shops, reaching customers in over 200 countries. Spotify delivers music as a direct download; Netflix streams films to the TV. Digital distribution cuts property costs, opens up international markets and runs 24/7. The downsides are delivery costs, high returns rates (fashion returns can reach 40%) and cyber-security. Many businesses now run both: Tesco has supermarkets AND groceries.com; Next has stores AND next.co.uk. This is called a multi-channel approach.

The choice depends on the target customer. ASOS goes pure digital because its teen-to-thirties shoppers live on their phones. Primark refuses to sell online at all — its low prices would be wiped out by delivery costs, and impulse-buying in store is central to its model. Greggs is almost entirely physical because a sausage roll needs to be eaten hot. Netflix is pure digital because streaming is the only sensible way to deliver a film. Most UK retailers now run both channels because customers expect the choice — John Lewis customers research online and buy in store, or buy online and return in store. Matching the channel to the customer matters more than running every channel at once.

Key Fact

OCR names two types of distribution: physical (shops, supermarkets, market stalls) and digital (websites, apps, downloads). The choice depends on the target customer, the product and the business’s costs.

For ‘Discuss’ and ‘Evaluate’ questions, weigh both sides: a new start-up could pick social media OR local print, and you need to say which beats the other for THIS business and why. No marks for unsupported judgements.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Promotion methods include point of sale, advertising across five channels, price reductions, loss leaders, competitions and free samples.
  • Place is split into physical distribution (shops) and digital distribution (websites, apps) — most UK businesses now use both.
  • The right mix depends on the target customer, the product, costs and the business’s objectives.

lessons.title: The Marketing Mix in Action
lessons.description: How the four Ps work as a system and how market data signals when the mix should change.
lessons.content_html:
Over the last few lessons we have looked at each of the four Ps — product, price, promotion and place — one at a time. Real businesses do not decide them one at a time. They work as a system. A change to the price affects the right promotion. A change to the place affects the target customer, which feeds back into the product. This lesson shows how the four Ps work together and how businesses read market data to decide when the mix needs to change.

The Four Ps as a System

The integrated marketing mix is the idea that the four Ps must reinforce each other. If they pull in different directions, customers get a confused message and sales suffer.

Apple is the textbook example. The product is premium (clean design, aluminium and glass), the price is premium (£1,000+ for a flagship iPhone), the promotion is sleek (minimal TV adverts, clean website), and the place is premium (Apple Stores on the best streets in London, Manchester and Liverpool plus apple.com). Every P says the same thing: ‘this is high-end’. If Apple suddenly started selling through Poundland, the whole brand image would collapse.

Primark — The Opposite Example

Primark aims at the opposite end of the UK market, and its mix is just as integrated. The product is cheap, fast-fashion basics. The price is the lowest on the high street. The promotion relies on word-of-mouth and shop-window displays rather than TV adverts. The place is big high-street stores in city centres, with deliberately no online sales — delivery costs would wipe out the margins on a £5 T-shirt. Every P says ‘cheap, cheerful, impulse-buy in store’, and that consistency is what makes the strategy work.

Key Fact

An integrated marketing mix is one where all four Ps — product, price, promotion and place — reinforce the same message for the target customer. Apple and Primark are both integrated, even though they target opposite ends of the market.

ASOS — Digital-First Mix

ASOS shows how all four Ps can lock together around a digital-first model. The product is on-trend fashion aimed at 18-to-34-year-olds. The price is competitive with Zara and H&M, with frequent student-discount offers. The promotion is heavy on Instagram and TikTok because that is where the target customer is. The place is 100% digital — a website and an app — because the target customer shops on their phone. If ASOS tried to run television adverts aimed at over-60s while keeping everything else the same, the mix would fall apart: the channel would not match the customer the other three Ps were designed for.

Reading the Market — Interpreting Data

The mix is never fixed. Customer behaviour, technology and rivals all keep moving, and businesses use market data to spot when a change is needed. Three common data signals are changes in demand, changes in market share, and the effect of promotion on sales.

Imagine a UK chocolate bar is selling 2 million units a week in 2023, 1.8 million in 2024 and 1.6 million in 2025. Demand has fallen 20% in two years. The mix needs attention. The business could refresh the product (new flavours, different packaging), cut the price to attract price-sensitive shoppers, promote more heavily (TV or social media relaunch), or change the place (push into smaller convenience stores). Data on its own does not decide — it tells the business that something is wrong and prompts a choice.

For years the UK supermarket market share was dominated by Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons. Between 2010 and the early 2020s Aldi and Lidl climbed from under 5% to roughly 18% combined. Tesco saw the data every quarter and had to respond: it launched the Aldi Price Match promotion (price), refreshed Clubcard (a promotion loyalty tool), expanded the Finest range (product) and pushed online delivery (place). All four Ps moved together — the mix had to change as a system, not one P at a time.

A coffee chain spends £50,000 on a two-week Instagram campaign. Weekly sales before the campaign averaged £200,000. During the campaign they climbed to £240,000 a week — a 20% lift. Afterwards sales settled at £210,000. The data tells the business two things: the campaign worked in the short term, and there is a small lasting lift even after the spend ended. The question for next time is whether £50,000 was the right amount — would £25,000 have achieved most of the effect? Data interpretation turns a marketing decision into a numbers-based judgement.

When Part of the Mix Falls Behind

Debenhams is a cautionary case. For years the product (mid-tier fashion) and price (mid-tier) stayed roughly the same while rivals like Next invested in e-commerce and ASOS captured the online segment. Debenhams’ place (mainly high-street stores) fell behind the market — the mix stopped being integrated because only three Ps were moving forward. The business fell into administration in 2020. When data shows one P dragging, the business has to decide quickly whether to invest in bringing it up to date or shrink to match the remaining strengths.

Key Fact

Market data signals — changes in demand, changes in market share and the measured effect of promotion — tell a business when the marketing mix needs to change. A good mix moves all four Ps together, not one at a time.

The Mix Follows the Customer

All of this comes back to one idea: the marketing mix exists to serve the target customer. Data tells the business what the customer is doing. The four Ps are the levers the business can pull in response. A mix that matches the customer — Apple for premium tech fans, Primark for value-led fashion, ASOS for digital-native Gen Z — keeps the business growing. A mix that drifts out of step with the customer loses market share quickly.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, you must move beyond describing the four Ps one by one. Show how each P supports the others and use numbers from the scenario (market share, sales, footfall) to back your judgement. For ‘Recommend’ questions, pick one mix change, justify it using the data, and explain why it beats at least one alternative in this business’s context. Approximately 10% of the paper is made up of quantitative skills, so always use the numbers in front of you.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four Ps must work together as an integrated mix — changing one usually means rethinking the others.
  • Market data (demand changes, market share changes, promotion results) signals when the mix needs to change.
  • A mix that matches the target customer drives growth; a mix that drifts out of step loses share quickly.

lessons.title: Organisational Structures & Ways of Working
lessons.description: Tall, flat and matrix structures, span of control, delegation and modern UK ways of working.
lessons.content_html:
Human resources (HR) is the business function that looks after people — recruiting them, organising them, motivating them and developing them. Every business, from a two-person coffee van to a supermarket chain, needs some way of showing who reports to whom and how people are employed. This lesson covers two OCR topics: organisational structures (tall, flat, matrix) and ways of working (full-time, part-time, flexible, temporary, remote and self-employed).

Why Structure Matters

An organisational structure sets out job roles, responsibilities and lines of communication. It decides how quickly an instruction travels, who is allowed to make which decision, and how many people each manager supervises. Get it right and the business runs smoothly; get it wrong and instructions get lost, staff feel unclear on their role, and decisions take far too long.

Tall (Hierarchical) Structures

A tall structure has many layers of management. An NHS hospital trust is a clear example: a chief executive sits above directors, who sit above senior managers, ward managers and clinical staff. Each manager oversees only a handful of people, which means tight supervision and clear promotion paths — but decisions are slow because a message has to climb many rungs. Large, safety-critical organisations like the Royal Navy, the NHS and national banks tend to be tall because clear lines of responsibility matter more than speed.

Flat Structures

A flat structure has few layers. A tech start-up of twenty people might have a founder, one team of engineers and one team of marketers — that is it. Decisions happen fast, staff feel trusted and costs are lower because there are fewer managers to pay. The trade-off is that each manager supervises a lot of people, so they cannot give much individual attention. Start-ups and creative agencies usually run flat; they add layers as they grow.

Matrix Structures

A matrix structure mixes two reporting lines. An engineer at an engineering firm might report to both the ‘engineering department’ manager AND the manager of the specific project they are working on at the moment. This works well for businesses where project teams form and re-form — construction, consultancy, pharmaceuticals. Staff get the benefit of expert function managers plus hands-on project leadership. The risk is that two managers may pull in different directions, so clear rules on who decides what are essential.

Key Fact

Tall, flat and matrix are the three main structures. Tall suits large, safety-critical organisations; flat suits start-ups and small firms; matrix suits project-based businesses where teams re-form often.

Span of Control and Chain of Command

The span of control is the number of people a single manager oversees. A narrow span (three or four staff) allows close mentoring; a wide span (fifteen or more) demands that workers manage themselves. The chain of command is the route an instruction travels from the top of the business to the bottom. A long chain means careful control; a short chain means fewer people reword the message, so it arrives clearly.

Delegation, Subordinates and Authority

Delegation is when a manager hands a task, and the authority to complete it, to a subordinate further down the chain. A supermarket duty manager might delegate a promotional display to a supervisor. Good delegation motivates staff by showing trust, develops skills and frees managers for bigger decisions. Poor delegation — giving someone a task without the authority to decide, or without proper training — causes mistakes and resentment. The manager stays accountable even after delegating; handing the task over is not the same as handing over the responsibility.

There is no perfect structure. A two-person coffee van does not need an org chart at all, just a clear split of tasks. A national retailer with hundreds of sites needs a taller structure so that all shops follow the same standards. Fast-moving sectors like fashion and tech tend to stay flat so they can respond quickly to customers; regulated sectors like banking and healthcare tend to stay taller so risks are controlled. Matrix fits project-based businesses like consultancies, construction firms and pharmaceutical research teams where the same employee contributes to several projects at once.

Ways of Working

Once the business has a shape, it also has choices about how people are actually employed. OCR names several ways of working that have become common in UK businesses.

  • Full-time — usually 35 to 40 hours a week. Gives the business a committed worker and the employee a stable income and holiday pay. Used for most core roles at M&S and Tesco.
  • Part-time — fewer hours, often pro-rata pay and benefits. Helps parents, students and carers stay in work and helps businesses match staffing to demand — a café can run three staff at lunchtime and one mid-afternoon.
  • Temporary — a fixed-term or casual arrangement, common at Christmas (Royal Mail hires thousands of seasonal sorters) or during exam marking.
  • Zero-hour — no guaranteed hours; workers are called in as needed. Common in hospitality and retail. Gives businesses maximum flexibility but leaves workers with no guaranteed income.
  • Flexible working — staggered hours, compressed weeks, or flexi-time. Helps staff balance work and life, which can improve retention.
  • Working from home / remote working — the employee does the job from home or another location, using a laptop and internet. Exploded in use after 2020. Cuts commuting and can cut office rent, but makes teamwork and training harder.
  • Self-employed — the worker is their own boss (a freelance designer, a plumber, a market trader). Not an employee of the business at all — hired for specific jobs and paid per invoice.

The right mix of ways of working helps a business control costs and attract the right people. A supermarket might use full-time staff for managers, part-time staff for evenings and weekends, and seasonal temporary staff for Christmas. A software firm might use full-time engineers, flexible home-working, and self-employed specialists for one-off design jobs. Ways of working also affect morale — staff who are offered flexibility tend to stay longer, which lowers recruitment costs. Overuse of zero-hour contracts or temporary work can hurt the brand as an employer, so businesses balance flexibility against stability.

Key Fact

OCR names full-time, part-time, temporary, zero-hour, flexible, working from home / remote, and self-employed as the main ways of working. Each balances flexibility for the business against security for the worker.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on structure, match the structure to the business in the scenario — a fast-growing start-up is not run like an NHS trust. For ‘Discuss’ questions on ways of working, weigh the benefit to the business against the cost to the employee. ‘Analyse’ questions reward chains of reasoning: tall structure → clear supervision → fewer errors in a safety-critical setting → stronger reputation. Always tie your answer to a feature of the business in the case study.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Tall, flat and matrix are the three main structures — each suits different types of business.
  • Span of control, chain of command, delegation, subordinates and authority all describe how decisions and instructions move through a business.
  • OCR names seven ways of working — full-time, part-time, temporary, zero-hour, flexible, remote and self-employed — and each balances flexibility against security.

lessons.title: Recruitment, Motivation, Training & Employment Law
lessons.description: Recruiting, motivating, training and developing staff — plus the key UK employment laws.
lessons.content_html:
People are the most expensive resource most businesses buy — and the most valuable. This lesson pulls together four linked HR topics: how businesses recruit and select the right person, how they motivate staff once they arrive, how they train and develop them, and the employment laws that protect workers. One dense lesson because each topic is short, but the connections between them matter.

Why Businesses Recruit

A business needs to recruit for three main reasons: to replace an employee who has left, to cope with business growth (more customers, new sites, new products), or to fill a skill gap the current team cannot cover. A Manchester café that expands from one site to three needs new baristas. A tech firm switching to AI needs engineers it cannot grow internally. A retailer losing staff to a rival needs replacements quickly or service suffers.

Internal vs External Recruitment

Internal recruitment fills the vacancy from existing staff. John Lewis, the employee-owned department store, often promotes partners from the shop floor into management roles. Internal recruits know the culture, so induction is shorter and cheaper, and promoting from within motivates the rest of the team. External recruitment hires from outside — through adverts, agencies, social media or job sites. External applicants bring fresh skills and ideas but cost more in advertising fees, induction time and the risk of a bad fit.

Key Fact

Internal recruitment is faster, cheaper and motivates existing staff, but creates another vacancy and limits fresh ideas. External recruitment widens the talent pool but costs more and takes longer.

The Selection Process

Selection starts with a job description (what the post-holder will do) and a person specification (the skills and qualities the ideal candidate needs). The vacancy is advertised, applicants send a CV or fill in an application form, and the best candidates are invited to the next stage.

Common methods include the CV (candidate’s written summary of experience), application form (business-designed questions), interview (face-to-face or online questioning), tests (skills tests at Dyson, coding challenges at software firms), group activities (graduate schemes at PwC use team problem-solving), and references from previous employers as the final check before an offer. Businesses often use several methods together because a single interview can miss bad hires — good talkers are not always good workers.

Motivation — Why It Matters

Motivation is why employees turn up, try hard and stay. A motivated team produces more, makes fewer errors and gives better customer service. Demotivated staff are absent more often, leave more quickly and provide poorer service — which raises recruitment costs and lowers profit.

Financial Motivation

Money matters. Financial motivation covers pay (the basic wage or salary), bonuses (extra pay for hitting a target — quarterly at banks, seasonal at retailers), profit sharing (staff receive a share of profits — John Lewis pays a partnership bonus based on annual profit), and fringe benefits (non-cash perks such as company cars, gym membership, staff discount). Fringe benefits can be very effective: a Tesco 10% staff discount costs Tesco very little but feels valuable to employees.

Non-Financial Motivation

Non-financial motivation covers praise, recognition, varied work and responsibility. OCR names specific methods: job rotation (moving an employee between different jobs to reduce boredom and widen skills), job enrichment (adding more responsibility and challenge to an existing job), team-working (organising work around small teams with shared goals), award schemes (Employee of the Month), a positive working environment (good lighting, safe kit, respectful managers), and praise from managers and peers. These methods are often cheaper than pay rises and can have a bigger long-term effect on employee retention.

OCR examiners have flagged this as the single most common wrong answer on this topic. Read it twice.

Training is relatively short-term and narrow — teaching a specific skill for a current role. A new barista learning to use the coffee machine. A shop assistant learning to work the till.

Staff development is longer-term and wider-ranging — preparing an employee to progress. Vocational qualifications, apprenticeships, leadership courses, or secondments to other departments. Development looks beyond today’s job to tomorrow’s career. If a question asks about staff development, do not write about till training. If it asks about training, do not launch into apprenticeships lasting three years.

Training Methods

Training starts with induction — the introduction given when an employee first joins, covering company policies, health and safety, job basics and introductions to colleagues. After that, OCR names two ongoing types: on-the-job training (learning while doing the real work, shadowing a colleague, coached by a supervisor) and off-the-job training (away from the normal workplace — a classroom course, an external training provider, an online module). On-the-job is cheap and directly relevant; off-the-job is more expensive but can bring in expert knowledge the business does not have internally.

Staff Development

Staff development prepares people for bigger roles. Vocational qualifications (NVQs, BTECs, City & Guilds) build career-long skills. Apprenticeships combine paid work with study — BT, BAE Systems and the NHS all run large apprenticeship programmes. Good staff development raises retention because employees see a future in the business.

Employment Law

UK law sets minimum rules that every business must follow. OCR names four areas you should know.

  • Minimum wage — the lowest hourly pay allowed by law. The National Minimum Wage / National Living Wage is reviewed every April. Employers who underpay face fines and naming-and-shaming by HMRC.
  • Contracts — every UK employee has a legal right to a written statement of their main job terms on or before their first day. It covers hours, pay, holiday entitlement and notice periods.
  • Holidays and hours of work — full-time workers are entitled to at least 5.6 weeks paid holiday a year. The Working Time Regulations cap the average working week at 48 hours unless the worker chooses to opt out.
  • Equality and discrimination — the Equality Act protects workers from being treated unfairly because of age, sex, race, disability, religion, pregnancy or sexual orientation. Discrimination in recruitment, pay, training or promotion is unlawful and can lead to Employment Tribunal claims.
Key Fact

OCR names four key areas of employment law: minimum wage, the right to a contract, holidays and hours of work, and protection from discrimination. All UK businesses must follow these — getting them wrong risks fines, tribunal claims and reputation damage.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Read ‘training’ and ‘staff development’ questions very carefully — OCR examiner reports flag this as the most common mistake. Training is narrow and short-term (till skills). Development is wider and longer-term (NVQ, apprenticeship, career progression). For ‘Analyse’ questions on motivation, build a chain: method → effect on effort → effect on productivity/retention → effect on the business. For employment law questions, name the specific protection and link it to the scenario — an ‘Evaluate’ answer needs a supported judgement, not a summary.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Businesses recruit to replace leavers, grow, or fill skill gaps — through internal or external routes and a selection process using CVs, interviews, tests and references.
  • Motivation has financial methods (pay, bonus, profit share, fringe benefits) and non-financial methods (praise, job rotation, enrichment, team-working). Both raise retention.
  • Training builds a specific skill for the current job; staff development prepares employees for future roles. UK employment law sets rules on minimum wage, contracts, holidays, hours and discrimination.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct letter (D) clearly indicated. Secure: Correct letter selected. Developing: Incorrect letter. Emerging: No response. (1 mark for D.)

practice_questions.text: Identify one method of selection a business could use alongside an interview.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names one valid method precisely (test, group activity, presentation, references, CV screen). Secure: Names a valid method. Developing: Names something unrelated (e.g. job advert). Emerging: No valid response. (1 mark.)

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between training and staff development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear point — training is short-term/narrow for the current role (1); development is longer-term/wider for future progression such as qualifications or apprenticeships (1). Secure: Distinction made but one side thinner. Developing: One side only or muddled. Emerging: No valid distinction. (2 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a UK retailer of promoting internally rather than externally when filling a store manager role.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a benefit (e.g. faster, cheaper, motivates remaining staff) (1), applies to a UK retailer (1), develops with a ‘because’ clause (the promoted staff member already knows the store’s customers and processes) (1). Secure: Two elements. Developing: Knowledge only. Emerging: No relevant response. (3 marks.)

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK café chain of offering both financial (bonus) and non-financial (praise, job rotation) motivation methods.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Sustained chain — bonus rewards short-term sales targets → increases effort; non-financial methods reduce boredom and build belonging → raises retention → reduces recruitment cost overall. Applied to a café chain. Recognises trade-off (cost of bonus vs cheaper non-financial methods). Secure (3-4): Chain with some application. Developing (1-2): Descriptive list. Emerging (0): No relevant analysis. (6 marks.)

practice_questions.text: A fast-growing UK software firm must decide whether to invest most of its HR budget in short-term training courses or in longer-term staff development programmes such as apprenticeships and funded qualifications. Recommend which approach it should prioritise. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Clear recommendation with two developed reasons applied to a fast-growing software firm (e.g. apprenticeships build a pipeline of engineers as the firm scales), weighs at least one counter-point (short-term training is cheaper and fills immediate skill gaps), supported judgement tied to scenario, and correctly distinguishes training from development throughout. Secure (7-9): Recommendation with application and some evaluation. Developing (4-6): Recommendation with limited application, or confuses training and development. Emerging (1-3): Generic answer. (12 marks.)
